o1.biggest_strength: Every number ties back to my table, every move is ranked by trials, and Week 1 is literal enough that the writer starts Monday with a title, a meta description, an outline order and a publish date.
o1.biggest_mistake: Tells the writer to leave the decaying blog posts live and unchanged, so it never delivers the consolidation/redirect I asked for, and does nothing about the 22,500 lost blog clicks except walk away.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: A consolidation step for the 140 blog posts (merge or redirect the zero-click ones into the comparison and cookies pages) instead of 'leave them alone', plus a narrower projection range on the cookie-banner/privacy-page move so I can plan against a single number.

o2.biggest_strength: Normalising every page group to trials per 1,000 clicks, then deriving each move from my own CTR benchmarks and labelling the totals as ceilings with a note that rankings take weeks to land.
o2.biggest_mistake: Wednesday of week 1 tells the writer to send the draft to me for a facts check, when I said I am not available for questions, so the Monday start stalls on a dependency that does not exist.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Hand over the actual title, meta description and section order instead of describing them, drop the owner facts-check step, and write it in our voice rather than in benchmark-and-ceiling consultant shorthand.

reason: Both do the maths right and both put the writer on comparison pages, but 1 I could hand to the writer as it stands, in our voice, while 2 reads like a sharp analyst's deck that still needs the copy written and wrongly assumes I am around to sign off facts.
